meta.one_idea: split() cuts one string into a list of pieces and join() glues a list of strings back into one. A negative index counts from the end, and a negative step walks a list or a string backwards.
outcomes: Predict what split() gives with no separator, with a comma, and with a space, including the empty pieces.
Glue a list of strings into one string with join(), and say why a list of numbers fails.
Read any item from the end with a negative index, like list_a[-1].
Predict a slice with a negative step, and spot one that gives an empty list.
Reverse a list or a string with [::-1].

The deck agenda. The spine agenda S-AGENDA replaces it.

Build-up of slide 19. C4 steps it.
The question twin of slide 21. It is the ask press of E1.

Out of bounds in a slice. One spoken line in the guide, after C11 (see defects).

Build-up and question twins of slides 44 and 47. C12 steps them.
Negative slice and negative step on a string. Same rules as the list. One spoken line in the guide after C14.
The question twin of slide 53. It is the ask press of C14.
Bullet takeaways. Replaced by the example board K1.

defects: "Negative step requires the start to be greater than end" is true for positions from the front only. msgs[-1:1:-1] has start -1, smaller than 1, and still prints ['canteen', 'where?', 'ok'].
E2 says the start must be to the RIGHT of the stop. The exit X1 tests exactly this case.
"While slicing, index can go out of bounds" is right, but a student reads it as true for indexing too. list_a[-6] on a 5 item list stops with IndexError: list index out of range.
Slide 37 is a spoken line in the guide, and the guide says that indexing out of bounds is an error.
notes: The room is 50 to 60 first-year students on laptops. Laptops stay shut except on T1, T2 and the classroom quiz.
Votes are taken option by option: the instructor reads each option and asks how many think it is that one. Hands up. Nobody is named.

One picture for the first half: a string is a row of letter tiles, and split() cuts it where the separator sits. Every piece drops into a list box, an empty piece too, drawn as an empty box with ''. Use it on C2 to C7 and on G1.
One picture for the second half: a row of boxes with TWO position rows under it, 0 1 2 3 4 and -5 -4 -3 -2 -1. Use it on C9 to C14, E2 and X1. A cursor moves along it.
Python prints a list of strings in single quotes: ['1', '2']. Copy outputs from the JSON exactly; never turn them into double quotes.
Nothing before the title card may say the session's name. The hook may show Google Keep's own labels.
The bar to beat is Plans/DSA/Module 3 - Stacks & Queues/01 - Introduction to Stacks/: a simulation the room drives, a picture that refuses to lie.

build_contract: One self-contained HTML file. It opens offline from a USB stick and makes no network request.
It opens in presenter view. There is no sidebar, top bar or button the instructor has to use.

Right arrow or the clicker is one press. Left arrow goes back one press. F goes full screen, A shows all the cards, and End shows the whole card at once. The instructor guide tells the instructor these keys, so they must work.
Every card is its own screen, in the order of this spec. Press 1 is what shows when the card opens.
Every card's outer element carries data-spec="<card id>" and data-presses="<number of presses>". The review script reads both.
No link to any other file. The students' handout and the instructor guide are separate files, and a link from this file is how a class finds the answers.
rules: No autoplay. Nothing moves on a timer. One press, one move, with a caption that says what just happened.
Commit, then reveal. Where a card asks a question, the answer shows only on the press after the room has answered.
Wrong answers stay private. No names, no per-student results on screen. Hands are counted out loud, never shown.
The topic is named once. Nothing before the title card says today's topic, not a heading, not a caption, not a file name on a code card.

Words are exact. Words in quotation marks, and every line under Exact words, are final. The rest of a press describes what happens, in your own design. If an exact line does not fit, ask for a new one; do not rewrite it.
Code is exact. Copy code and outputs from the JSON, never retype them. Every output here came from running the program.
Simple English. Short sentences, everyday words. No em-dashes anywhere, the page title included.
Every card moves. A card that introduces an idea steps; a static card is a picture of a lecture.

beats.name: Hook 2: the latest message in the chat

cards.title: The latest message
cards.purpose: Feel why counting from the end is worth having: the latest message is always last, but its position from the top keeps changing. The long way is written out and run before the short way.
cards.heading: Which message is the latest?
show: Which message is the latest? What is its position?
A new message. Now which position?
The long way: count them all, then take one off.
WhatsApp never counts from the top. It goes to the end.

code.src:
chat = ['Lunch at 1?', 'ok', 'Canteen or mess?', 'Canteen']
chat += ["Coming in 5 mins"]
print(chat[len(chat) - 1])

chat = ['Lunch at 1?', 'ok', 'Canteen or mess?', 'Canteen']
chat += ["Coming in 5 mins"]
print(chat[-1])

presses.screen: A phone with WhatsApp open on a group, <q>Lunch gang</q>, with the four messages in data.chat, newest at the bottom. Small grey positions 0 to 3 beside them. Caption: <q>Which message is the latest? What is its position?</q>

presses.screen: A new message slides in at the bottom: <q>Coming in 5 mins</q>. Its position shows 4. Caption: <q>A new message. Now which position?</q>
presses.say: Every new message moves the latest one down.

presses.screen: Beside the phone, latest_long.py, line 2 the biggest text: <q>print(chat[len(chat) - 1])</q>. It prints <q>Canteen</q>. Then latest_long_new.py, with the new message added, prints <q>Coming in 5 mins</q>. Caption: <q>The long way: count them all, then take one off.</q>
presses.say: len, a minus, a 1, brackets. Every time.

presses.screen: On the phone, new grey numbers appear from the bottom up: -1 beside the newest, -2 above it, and so on. Caption: <q>WhatsApp never counts from the top. It goes to the end.</q>
